The game is quirky at times, but so far I love it.

It is one of those passion projects which might be finished in decade or never, but even in current state offers dozens of hours of fun.

My first impressions:
-The building system is like Surviving Mars but you  place the walls, staircases, doors. You can make one big building with multiple stories or a bunch of smaller buildings.
-Trading system is similar to Port Royale with orbits instead of distance.
-Diplomacy system similar to XCOM, you depend on it entirely.
-If you play this with the lowest graphic settings, it doesn't necessarily look bad, it just becomes pixelized and it looks a bit like the old school master of orion. This is the first time i see a game that becomes "vintage" when on the lowest settings.

This was just released as early access and is very much unfinished, everything I mentioned is clunky and unpolished, so I will adjust my review according to future updates. But the things that are offered by this game would be uniquely awesome so the 15$ is completely worth the gamble for me.

Heavy duty space Colony SIm

Hidden gem, exactly what Kerbal Space Program could've been. A slight learning curve from the get-go, but once you get the idea and start making some money from contracts, it all falls together. in-depth colonial base construction and management, orbital station and ship assembly, rich tech tree and every notable terrestrial body in the solar system is there to colonize. You can build a colony on, or in orbit around, the Moon and Mars from the start. Other planets or moons require custom construction of ships from a settled location to furbish a colonization effort. Colonists have needs, traits, leadership/follower mentalities, and political leanings that lead into macro-scale politics for when colonies turn into their own independent polities. You can make a huge, complex colony, an interstellar human ant farm, exactly as the trailer and screenshots show.

The most Incredible part is that this was all made by a lone developer.

My first impression was being completely blown away. I expected a cool looking, but in the end disappointingly shallow colony sim. My bar for physical accuracy and depth in scifi games is pretty dang high to be fair, which is why most games can't meet what i want - but surprisingly, i was not disappointed here. You have mining with resources depending on the planetary body and densities varying depending on where exactly you build a base, complex crafting chains, needing to tend to colonists' needs, interplanetary logistics - it's kind of everything i wanted. More than i hoped for. If you like me look at the screenshots and immediately start salivating - yes, that's exactly what the game is.

With that said, it's certainly not perfect. The UI is pretty atrocious in particular, having the information you want on display is a fight and really you can't have much information available at a glance no matter what you do. I'm pretty sure you simply cannot manually rearrange windows, so all you can do is choose to minimize some but not others. It doesn't take a lot of open windows before some important info like your stored materials (arguably one of the most important info for an outpost) is completely invisible, because it's reduced to a tiny window with a scroll bar. Literally the info you need most gets treated as if it's one of the least important ones. Yikes! Be prepared to have to manage windows and/or scroll literally every time you need to check if you have resources for something.
And it's generally just very difficult figuring out where you can build what, how you make certain materials, how fast your research speed is going to be etc. You'll have to just figure these things out, the first few hours are not fun because of this. A lot of the time, you literally cannot even see the name of an object! Once again, it's impressively bad.
It's also otherwise not problem free, research sometimes just stops for no reason. Exiting the research screen for some reason freezes the game for a few seconds. Nothing too major so far, and any issues like this that i encountered honestly are barely worth mentioning given the UI elephant in the habitat.

I'm also not too far into the game to be fair, still just working on a lunar outpost. But i think i've seen enough to know where things are heading.

The one good news is that the dev is aware of the UI being atrocious, and a redesign is planned for the future. Generally it looks like the game is in fact being actively worked on and the dev cares, which is good to see - this looks like a genuine good use of Early Access from what i can tell. Still, this review talks about what the game is right now, not what it might one day be.

And with that, i can only really recommend it for hardcore scifi fans that are willing to deal with a really bad UI. There is a diamond in the rough here, but it's one of the roughest diamonds you'll ever see. And even if you are in the target audience and very excited for this game, like me, you may be better off waiting for said update and hopefully you'll be able to have a much more pleasant experience.

And to the dev - keep it up! I really really *really* want to see this game get more user friendly and otherwise to a place where i can wholeheartedly recommend it, because what i can see of this game now it absolutely has potential to be by far the best game in its niche, and i'm very excited.

Originally I came at this game with a scathing review, but after comments from the developer and joining the game's Discord I have come around on the game. This game comes with a heavy initial challenge but after you have a knack for raising the initial capital it becomes an interesting dive into our solar system.

However, if you decide you want to try this game out, there are a few recommendations I'd make:

1) Immediately opt into the beta - the game does have some UI issues that are addressed pretty well in this pretty stable beta. During several hours of play I only experienced a few issues that were fixed either by toggling between solar system and station view, reloading the save, or restarting the game

2) Remember this game is VERY young - There is a lot of customization of the look and feel of your bases/ships but more to be desired. After the initial challenge things get pretty easy, but adjustments to that are in the roadmap and there are a lot of improvements on the roadmap to come.

3) When fulfilling contracts, build the bare minimum, and build out as much as possible before bringing in colonists - The beta has rooms that function more like a barracks where you can cram beds into small spaces and save on materials, which means you get to walk away with a lot more of the signing money. Ideally you want to bring in the colonists as the last possible steps and transfer that bad boy immediately, but for your very first base you want to build a research room and ride out as much of the contract as possible to climb the tech tree (and maybe sign some research contracts along the way) If you can secure a few million credits profit from your first contract, it gets much easier to start building your own facilities and climb the tech tree, which makes everything much easier.

I will repeat: this game is early access and has a long way to go. But, it does satisfy a niche of space exploration mixed with colony management, and I think it's worth giving a go.

The building system is one of the best I've seen so far, allowing you to do pretty much whatever you want in term of planet based stations, orbital stations and interplanetary ships. Whether you want it to be beautiful, or functional, or both, you can do it quite easily. There's already hundreds of functional and decorative items, from kitchen, to science, to ressource production, with a pleasant emphasis on the science behind all of it. 

It already has in-depth mechanics like diplomacy, goods shortages, and (non-functional yet) radiation levels, underlining the challenges posed by interplanetary travel.

I'm really impressed by what the dev considers ''good enough'' and from what i've seen, I have no doubt he'll go on and offer us an ever better game. 

Beware now ! This game IS in early access and some of the things I listed above might make you feel that you've juste been robbed. But if you want to invest on a promising sandbox space-based game... Solargene might be it.

This game checked all my boxes so I gave it a shot. I plan to do a more lengthy review in the future but for now I think the main considerations are: 

It's an interesting "sandbox-like" station/colony builder survival (mainly just power/food/resources). I appreciate the realistic approach to docking and animations, as well as the unique system it offers for an enjoyable sandbox in the home Sol system.

It has your standard "necessary" logistic things such as production/consumption limits, but doesn't appear to place any indication on priority (as far as I am aware in the beginning tech stages)

Things I want to see improve.
1. The camera. It's insanely complex and tries to manage a "three-dimensional" system based on mouse hover location. This is rather cumbersome, but eventually you get used to it.
2. The UI - it's a bit "dumb." You have to manually close some opened windows, it's not very descriptive about what something is when you hover over it and I would love to be reminded near the object as to what that object or equipment is. Instead I have to click on it, go over to the new pop-up, and then scroll to see what it does or what resources it needs.
3. The tutorial is okay but a bit lacking. I would in the future hope to have the tutorial actually "set up" my initial station and spaceports on a new planet. Instead you have to somewhat "guess" how you do this even if an available contract needs 3 prior stations to be established.
4. I think it'd be neat for some of the contract ships you build to have a purpose later. Or would potentially become that spaceport to wherever you ship them to. Instead, contracts are just transferred over and basically are non existent after that.

Overall, I'm going to recommend it, since its worth the price and I enjoy seeing a developer's game come to fruition, even if it takes awhile for it to grow.

I bought this game because I was intrigued by the trailer, and because I wanted more realism in this genre after playing some other base building games. I am very happy with this game. Already in this early release state it has exceeded my expectations.

Actually it is possible to go to all 8 planets (sorry, Pluto) in the solar system and many of the major moons + procedural asteroids. They all have zoomed out global maps on a variable scale solar system map where you can select a base location anywhere on the surface of these worlds. This location loads what I assume is a semi-procedural very large surface map (multi km square) but limited with a realistic 3D sky box. After taking a loan it is then possible to build skyscraper sized bases! Interplanetary logistics requires building out space stations/ships, while shuttles link multiple bases together... That is only as far as I have got in a bit over 20 hours, but the scale of this game seems to be that if a solar empire!

Reading through the in-game tutorials is required as step 1, and there is still a steep learning-curve. There is also clearly room for development growth and polish, but so far this is a fantastic game. I look forward to playing more to unlock more features (I haven't even started research) and also seeing the game reach a "completed" state.

As a mature PC gamer (since the 8bit PC Commodore64 era) I have played many builder/management games and often get bored half way through 
- realising that all the rules and challenges are somewhat artificial and feel fake. 
This destroys my feeling of achievement and i often abandon the game having lost the incentive. 
Solargene despite being Early Access does feel very real, and that is rare these days.
Pros:
[ ] Solargene so far has been feeling more like a simulator and less than a game 
- despite it not being finished and needing structural integrity and more balancing. 
I love the feeling of real achievement even at this early stage of the game development.
[ ] The fact that it is very educational as a matter of process adds to the feeling of actual achievement.
Even if you "lose" you wont be as dumb as you was before  : ))
[ ] I enjoy the early start of a game - and often multiple starts, over and over once I learned a game mechanic the hard way  ...so I see multiple restarts as a learning curve - not failing. Life is like that often.
Cons:
[ ] User interface is clunky and mouse control awkward still.
[ ] Missing structural integrity takes away from the simulation credibility.
[ ] Popup windows of materials, prices, weights and store quantities should be un-dockable so  player can get a better overview when ordering shipments. The data needed to make ordering decisions is not available on one screen and required constant opening and closing  of windows which is very irritating.  

Summery:
I appreciate Alexander Semenovs's approach and integration of many complex but real life mechanics of engineering, science and biology and the balancing so far. 
Being the sole developer and publisher has the advantage that his vision for this game has not been watered down or compromised by others with a  different vision - and that is refreshing to see and 
I fully recommend this game/simulator even at the Early Access stage its more of a game than many ever will be.

Good strategy for moon start:
Building a moon base for a faction is a great way to get going but you actually have to give your base away to complete the contact.
Accept contract for whatever faction has a moon orbital station to make moon base.
Build bare bones base - minimal everything to meet contract. Focus on research and mining as those make you money. Dont worry about it being fully functional - just nobody starving, everyone got bed  and everyone has a job even if its useless. 
Meanwhile - build second base. This is the one you keep and make look good. You want to put it somewhere with as much helium as possible. The rest of the raw materials are nice to have but helium is where profit is. You refine the helium into fuel and 80-90 of those can sell for about 2 million. You also want a bit of ice for making water but helium refining will buy you everything else.
Stretch out the contract for as long as you can whilst you use the money you make from the 1st base to build second. Then transfer the 1st rubbish base over to fulfill contract just before it hits night.
If you do it well you will have a reasonable 2nd base already built and populated thats entirely yours to keep before you give up your 1st base.

The game is - as others described - massive and the tutorial lacking, though I find the latter less a hindrance than other, albeit small, things. To be honest I rather like the tutorial the way it is implemented - it's always there as a very basic help where you can jump around during the game without being intrusive. This is a very welcome change to a lot of other games, where you play half an hour babysitting tutorial which pumps a shitload of information into you that you don't need the first couple of hours just to have forgotten it when you progressed far enough to actually need it. With Solargene I ignored most of it right away and only opened it on demand, where it was always a good and compact help. 

The things that bother me most are pathfinding (as so often in games), weird dev choices and glitches, of which there are not much, but hell - I've got high standards and don't double down on them. First you start with no money whatsoever, and have to fulfill contracts, i.e. building a station, which you probably won't finish up in time to actually give it to the other party, which slams your reputation with them, but that is OK and easy to repair. Weird. And while building a massive station with multiple restaurants/charging stations/relaxation rooms/hospitals etc, settlers and robots oftentimes go out of their way to avoid the nearest one to fulfill their need but rather hike through the entire map to the farthest away, just to then glitch or get stuck at a stairway handle, door or other guy coming the other way. Annoying, but not breaking.

Speeeeeaking of maps: TF they are great. I mean in both detail and size. Building a station, you first decide for a colony spot with the ressource pattern of your choice and get thrown to the surface - mountains, valleys, hills - to search for your starting spot. Oh, that mountain in the distance looks nice - go there. I've seen no end to the map, which is just sooo cool, I felt like a boy that got presented with a puppy (Edith says: there is a map border, found it b/c I was curious after the review write, but then, we're speaking multiple square kilometers here...) Then you place your landing spots and shop for building materials, because that's what you were given money for. It is a little annoying that you need to start all over again with unlocking all rooms/buildings for every new colony (which does not help to shop for materials, b/c you don't know what you need, and shuttles are expensive like in RL), but at least you can easily move ressources between the colonies lateron. And of course your researched stuff is not being reset, just not available from the start (you first need to place a landing spot to unlock solar panels, build them to unlock batteries, build them to unlock an airlock... you get my point). Research also progresses nicely, with ever higher demand for facilities and computing power (both is needed, which I view as a great choice), and tourism I haven't yet started with. Oh, and of course there's different space agencies/nations, each with their own cuisine that the astronauts demand, which is also lovely. 

So, all in all, after about 30 hours of play, I can honestly say this game has already earned its spot on my favlist. It's complex, mostly realistic, and a challenge. Love that. Just please fix the pathfinding, I want to test the limits of your maps :D

This is an awesome game. Even in the current "beta" state it has well over 100 hours of entertainment value. The different planets and moons with their own day and night cycle, resources and different distance from the sun make for a nice diversity in game play.

For example on Moon you can easily use solar panels, but you will also need a lot of batteries to survive the 14-days lunar night. On Mars panels still work well and you'll need far fewer batteries, but power from panels will be somewhat reduced due to further distance from the sun. Further away solar panels are not a viable option and you'll need to develop nuclear and maybe fusion power (there is a research tree).

You can (and eventually will) build a vast network of planetary bases, space stations and even manned and unmanned ships flying between them or estabilishing new bases of operation. You can even mine asteroids in the main belt (and presumably also the Kuiper belt).

But you have to account for travel times due to the different orbits of all these places and that adds another layer of logistical complexity. You can research several new types of rocket propulsion (obviously some futuristic ones) and that will help with travel times.

Once you have set up space stations as transit hubs you can send shuttles between places to transport resources or people (astronauts and tourists). In the standard difficulty you don't have to manage fuel for these simple shuttles, just tell them what to transport from A to B - even shuttles with regular schedules are possible to set up supply chains.

Overall, this game is very enjoyable as is. There are very few bugs (I had only 2 crashes in 200 hours of play and it might have been due to currupt game files). The learning curve has some steepness in mid-game as not all of the tutorial is finished yet, but you'll find tips and help in the discussion forums and on the dev's Discord server.

I don't want to build any more multi-storied installations now after fighting with the visible floor system.  There's also maybe a gap or lack of difficulty/depth with full simulation elements -- ie. complicated atmospherics/mechanics you might see in Stationeers, Rimworld, or Space Station 13, but the game gives a wider breath of scope so it can certainly be forgiven or perhaps welcomed for not focusing too much on minutia at each individual station.

Indie dev has shown himself to have a great vision -- and he just received a grant from Epic; I'd expect this project to excel and improve.

It's a little clunky at times, but the interesting management system for resources and staff: which is based on semi-realistic resource distribution across our solar system (as we know now) sets up a very enjoyable slow buildup of your little company empire. Of course there are some game elements that helps make it playable instead of just years in space travel. In the end this is a slow space building management game, if you are interested in that you'll like this game.

TL;DR: It might be a nice game but the sub-par usability kills all the fun for me.  

I like playing everything that involves space and colony sim, so this looked quite appealing to me. On paper it ticks all the boxes. However the game's usability is so bad, that it kills all the fun for me. This starts with the suboptimal camera control (WASD is basically not usable as it scrolls way too fast) continues with hard to read icons especially for base building, missing tooltips, hard to read fonts etc.  It lacks even basic quality of life functions like buying the needed resources for a building without having to write the list of items down and then manually filling an order with all the items. 

The tutorial is just a few screens of text and while it is better than nothing, it's not integrated into the game. I can forgive this (I have played the X-series where tutorials are also not very well integrated into the game) if it would at least be servicable. At one point in the tutorial the game instructs you to buy stuff for your first colony buildings and gives you a rundown of what to buy. However when you open the buy menu, it overlaps the tutorial window and hides the information you need to enter. This just shows how usability is really not there at all. 

I want to focus on managing the growth and  success of my colony, not fight the UI. I want to make meaningful decisions, not hand-write and calculate the number of resources I need to buy on a sheet of paper to then enter them into a buy dialog. That really is monkeywork the game can do, there is no gameplay value whatsoever in it. 

The factions remain elusive, as a starting player I have no clue what the factions are good for and why I would want their favor.  It would probably also have been better to use some fictional factions rather than real existing countries, given the current world stage. I play space games to explore how a better future for mankind could look like - not to rehash the current, sad state of affairs on planet Earth.

Other negative points were the really annoying music (way too much bombast with the same 4 chords in different variations) and the less than great performance given the only ok-ish graphic fidelity.

So right now I cannot recommend this. This game needs a total overhaul of its usability so you can actually get to managing your colonies before being frustrated by the sub-par usability and it needs _something_ to pull the player in and interest him into what's going on. As it stands, there is no pull here that can make me overlook the usability. Given that there is only one developer behind this I also don't think the game will reach such a state anytime soon, so I chose to refund it. 

I would love to be wrong here as I really love playing everything space and colony sim.

There are whole dimensions of the game completely missing from the documentation, like how do you generate delta-V in a space station? (not mentioned at all in the tutorial, try googling it and you'll get something about kerbal space program.)

The developer should spend a lot more time on the tutorial. There is about 10 minutes worth of tutorial in this game that probably took less than 30 minutes to write. If the authors put a bit more time into it, the game would become exponentially more accessible, less frustrating and cause less refunds.

The answers may be available if you spend hours searching for them or joining a online chat, but honestly that shouldn't be necessary and I didn't buy this game to have a back-and-forth dialogue (with hours between messages) with random people on the internet about how to use basic mechanics of the game that should be documented in the tutorial. I have a full-time job, I want to sit down for an hour every day or two and play, not write to pen-pals over the internet.

I would also add that I consider myself to enjoy exploring and discovering game mechanics and believe I am fairly decent at it. But there is no guide or path to follow, and when you're stuck there is nothing to guide you. It is a shame because if the developer sat down for an hour and actually hammered out a wiki, or spent 10% of the time they do developing writing a tutorial, wiki or literally any form of documentation the game would benefit dramatically. In fact, if they literally just created and advertised a wiki in game, I'm sure the community would flesh it out for them. Instead, they have made basically zero effort on this front and have left you wondering aimlessly the mechanics of the game.

The game mechanics are interesting once you figure them out.

Unfortunately, can't recommend the game since the developers don't put any effort into the tutorial and you will probably just end up annoyed and wasting time.
